summary: The paper proposes the first quantum algorithm for constrained portfolio optimization by reducing the problem to a second‑order cone program and solving it with a quantum interior‑point method. The runtime is Õ(n^{1.5} κ ζ / δ² log(1/ε)) versus a practical classical complexity of about O(n^{3.5} log(1/ε)), suggesting a potential ~O(n) polynomial speedup if condition numbers remain bounded. Simulations on S&P‑500 historical data (50–100 assets, 10–500 day windows) estimate an empirical scaling exponent of about n^{2.387} (95% CI [2.184, 2.589]).

experiments.description: Numerical experiments evaluating the quantum short-step interior-point method for constrained portfolio optimization on real market data, including convergence behavior, condition number behavior, and estimated average-case complexity.

algorithm.variant: Quantum short-step interior-point method for constrained portfolio optimization via SOCP reduction
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Run for T = O(sqrt(r) log(n/epsilon)) iterations until duality gap <= epsilon

hyperparameters.sigma: 1 - 0.1/sqrt(r) in the classical IPM description; quantum analysis uses sigma = 1 - alpha/sqrt(r) with 0 < alpha <= 0.01
hyperparameters.n: size of Newton system / number of assets in the sampled instances

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Start from a strictly feasible initial point (x,y,s,nu) = (x,y,s,nu0)

optimizer_settings.tolerance: epsilon=0.1 in experiments; delta determined by tomography precision

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Portfolio optimization is reduced to an SOCP; the Newton linear systems are solved via quantum linear system solving with QRAM-based block encodings. No QUBO/binary encoding is used.
problem_formulation.objective_function: minimize x^T Sigma x subject to mu^T x = R and x >= 0; in the SOCP form, minimize (1,0)^T(t;x) with constraints enforcing t = Mx, mu^T x = R, Ax = b, and positivity via Lorentz cones
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: SOCP constraints with Lorentz cones; positivity enforced by second-order cone constraints; equality constraints handled in the Newton system; tomography-induced approximation error bounded by delta

problem_instance.description: Portfolio optimization on historical stock-return data from the cvxportfolio repository; experiments use subsets of S&P-500 companies and varying time windows
problem_instance.dataset_name: cvxportfolio repository / S&P-500 historical stock data

dataset_specification.description: Historical data for S&P-500 companies over 2007-2016; subsampled to 50 companies for one set of experiments and 100 random companies for scaling experiments; random subintervals of length t in [10,500]

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Compute mean returns mu and matrix M from historical prices/returns; use the square root of the covariance matrix Sigma = M^T M; fix epsilon = 0.1 for scaling experiments
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Simulate the algorithm with added Gaussian noise corresponding to tomography precision; compare classical (noise-free) and quantum-noisy convergence; record duality gap, tomography precision, condition number, and estimated complexity; fit power laws and report confidence intervals

noise_model.noise_type: Gaussian noise added to simulate tomography precision

noise_parameters.tomography_precision: used as noise magnitude; exact numeric value not specified

implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical short-step interior-point method / SOCP solver baseline
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Compute mu and M from the dataset; build SOCP constraint matrices; sample random subsets and time windows for scaling study
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Recover portfolio solution x from the SOCP solution; fit power laws to observed parameter scaling

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: duality gap decreases multiplicatively; quantum and classical curves are similar

results.value: no observable growth with problem size; large only in a small number of instances

classical_baselines.value: theory suggests κ grows as 1/ν, but experiments show this upper bound is not attained

speedup_claims.factor: polynomial speedup; potentially O(n) speedup in practice
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical short-step interior-point method / practical SOCP solvers
speedup_claims.conditions: assuming bounded condition number κ and not-too-small tomography precision δ; especially when n is large and r is small
speedup_claims.caveats: The quantum runtime depends on κ, ζ, and 1/δ^2; the paper reports simulations and fitted scaling, not a physical QPU implementation.

speedup_claims.factor: approximately O(n) speedup; observed complexity O(n^2.387) vs practical O(n^3.5)
speedup_claims.conditions: for most instances in the sampled cvxportfolio-based experiments, after removing 1% largest outliers
speedup_claims.caveats: This is based on fitted power laws from simulated algorithm runs, not hardware execution.

speedup_claims.factor: O~(n^(omega+0.5)) classical vs O~(n^1.5 zeta kappa / delta^2) quantum
speedup_claims.baseline_method: best classical algorithms for constrained portfolio optimization
speedup_claims.conditions: moderately accurate solution; bounded κ and moderate δ
speedup_claims.caveats: The advantage is conditional on problem-dependent parameters and QRAM/block-encoding assumptions.

complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O~(n^{omega+0.5} log(1/epsilon)) ; in practice about O(n^{3.5} log(1/epsilon))

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires large-scale fault‑tolerant quantum computers implementing quantum linear system solvers with QRAM data structures and efficient block encodings for matrices of size n (assets). Runtime T = Õ(√r log(n/ε) · n κ ζ / δ²).
limiting_factors: Dependence on QRAM for block‑encoding access to matrices
Need for fault‑tolerant quantum linear system solvers
Condition number κ and tomography precision δ strongly affect runtime

notes: No physical QPU or gate-based circuit experiment is reported; the paper presents numerical simulations of the quantum algorithm and theoretical resource estimates. num_qubits is not explicitly given because the algorithm is described at the linear-system / QRAM level rather than as a fixed circuit.

The paper claims a polynomial speedup (potentially O(n) in practice) compared with classical SOCP interior‑point methods, but only provides theoretical complexity analysis and classical simulations of convergence behavior.
